posts.prompt: What did they say this week that you want to remember exactly?
posts.caption: The exact words go first. In a month you'll have the gist, the funny idea, the general shape — but not the wording. Write it down the way they said it, grammar mistakes and all.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading QUESTION above the prompt: "What did they say this week that you want to remember exactly?"

posts.prompt: Photograph their hands. Just their hands.
posts.caption: Faces you have thousands of. Hands you have almost none. The scab on the knuckle, the marker stain, the way they hold a fork wrong. That's the part that changes fastest and gets photographed least.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading PHOTO above the prompt text: Photograph their hands. Just their hands.

posts.prompt: Film them telling you about their day. Don’t prompt them.
posts.caption: Unprompted, the order comes out strange. The dropped cracker before the field trip. That's the part you'd never have thought to ask about, and the part you'll want back.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading VIDEO above the prompt text: Film them telling you about their day. Don't prompt them.

posts.prompt: Record them telling you a story. Any story. Don’t correct the words they say wrong.
posts.caption: The mispronunciations are the part you'll want later. The wrong word for hospital, the sentence that runs out of road halfway through. Fixing it now costs you the version you'd want to hear in ten years.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading VOICE above the prompt: "Record them telling you a story. Any story. Don't correct the words they say wrong."

posts.prompt: Never let go of the hug first today. Let them be the one to pull away.
posts.caption: Most hugs end on your schedule. This one won't. Some kids let go in two seconds, some hang on long enough that you notice something. Either way, you learn the length of it.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading ACTIVITY above the prompt: "Never let go of the hug first today. Let them be the one to pull away."

posts.prompt: Write them something about money that you wish someone had told you at nineteen.
posts.caption: Most money advice ages badly. What holds up is the specific thing you got wrong at nineteen and how long it took to notice. Write that part. They can decide later what to do with it.
posts.altText: A cream card with a small badge reading LETTER above the prompt: "Write them something about money that you wish someone had told you at nineteen."

posts.prompt: What are they obsessed with right now?
posts.caption: The obsession is usually specific and slightly ridiculous. Trash trucks. A particular blue cup. The word "actually." It will be gone in six weeks and you won't remember it happened unless you write it down.
posts.altText: Plain cream card with a small badge reading QUESTION above the prompt text: "What are they obsessed with right now?"

posts.prompt: Get down to their eye level and take the photo from there.
posts.caption: Most photos of your kid are taken from five feet above them. Crouch down and you get the room the way they actually live in it. Also their face straight on, not tilted up at you.
posts.altText: Cream-colored card with a small badge reading PHOTO above the prompt text: "Get down to their eye level and take the photo from there."

posts.prompt: Ask them ten questions about their mom and film the answers. Don’t correct anything.
posts.caption: The wrong answers are the good part. Your age, your job, your favorite food — all of it filtered through someone four feet tall. Let it stand. In a year you'll want the version they believed.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading VIDEO above the prompt: "Ask them ten questions about their mom and film the answers. Don't correct anything."

posts.prompt: Record them singing. Whatever they’re singing.
posts.caption: The made-up verses. The wrong lyrics they're sure are right. You will not remember what that voice sounded like, and thirty seconds is enough to keep it.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading VOICE above the prompt: "Record them singing. Whatever they're singing."

posts.prompt: Get on the floor for ten minutes. That’s the whole mission.
posts.caption: Ten minutes on the floor changes the angle. You end up hearing about the sticker under the couch, or the plan for the dinosaurs. Nobody has to say anything, either. That counts.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading ACTIVITY above the prompt: "Get on the floor for ten minutes. That's the whole mission."

posts.prompt: Write them a letter about exactly who they are right now. They won’t be this person next year.
posts.caption: Not who they're becoming. Who they are today, at this exact size, with this exact set of opinions about socks. Write it down plain. In a year you'll read it and be surprised by how much you'd already forgotten.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading LETTER above the prompt: "Write them a letter about exactly who they are right now. They won't be this person next year."

posts.prompt: What do they call you? Write down every version.
posts.caption: There's the one on the birth certificate and then there's whatever they landed on at fourteen months. The mispronunciations, the singsong one, the one they use only when they want something. Those get replaced without warning.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading QUESTION above the prompt text: "What do they call you? Write down every version."

posts.prompt: Photograph their shoes by the door.
posts.caption: Nobody photographs the shoes. But the size changes every few months, and the way they get kicked off says more than a posed picture would. Takes ten seconds on your way past.
posts.altText: A cream card with a small badge reading PHOTO above the prompt text: "Photograph their shoes by the door."

posts.prompt: Film them doing the thing they’re currently best at.
posts.caption: Right now it's probably something small. Peeling a clementine in one strip. Climbing onto the counter without a sound. Skills expire quietly, and nobody announces the last time.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading VIDEO above the prompt text: Film them doing the thing they're currently best at.

posts.prompt: Record them counting as high as they can go.
posts.caption: They'll stall somewhere. Twenty-nine, or that stretch in the sixties where the words run out. The stall is the part you'll want later, along with the breath they take before trying again.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading VOICE above the prompt text: "Record them counting as high as they can go."

posts.prompt: Carry them when they ask, even though they can walk fine.
posts.caption: They can walk. They ask anyway. Ten years from now you won't remember the errand, but you might remember the weight of them on your hip and the exact spot their chin landed.
posts.altText: Plain cream card with a small badge reading ACTIVITY above the prompt: "Carry them when they ask, even though they can walk fine."

posts.prompt: Write down what you were afraid of before they were born, and what actually happened.
posts.caption: Most of the fears never showed up. The real one was something you'd never thought to worry about. Worth having both on paper, in your handwriting, before the list blurs.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading LETTER above the prompt text: Write down what you were afraid of before they were born, and what actually happened.

posts.prompt: What’s the bedtime routine right now, step by step?
posts.caption: The order matters to them and you know it by heart. Two books, then the hallway light at the exact angle. In a year it'll be different and you won't notice the day it changed. Write down the steps while they're still automatic.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading QUESTION above the prompt: "What's the bedtime routine right now, step by step?"

posts.prompt: Take a picture of what they built today, however unimpressive.
posts.caption: Blocks that fell over. A fort made of two chairs and a towel. The building doesn't have to be good to be worth a photo — in six months you'll want the scale of it, the hands in the frame, the specific junk they chose.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading PHOTO above the prompt text: Take a picture of what they built today, however unimpressive.

posts.prompt: Record thirty seconds of them just playing. No talking to the camera.
posts.caption: The narrated videos age strangely. The ones where nobody knows you're filming hold up. Thirty seconds of the humming, the sorting, the running commentary to no one.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading VIDEO above the prompt: "Record thirty seconds of them just playing. No talking to the camera."

posts.prompt: Record them saying the alphabet.
posts.caption: The alphabet is the excuse. What you're actually keeping is the wrong pause between L and M, the letter they add, the way they run out of breath by S. Six months from now that voice will be gone and you won't be able to say when it left.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading VOICE above the prompt text: Record them saying the alphabet.

posts.prompt: Use their oldest nickname out loud today, while they still answer to it.
posts.caption: The nicknames go quiet before anyone announces it. One day you say it and get a look instead of an answer. Say it now, and write down what came back.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading ACTIVITY above the prompt: "Use their oldest nickname out loud today, while they still answer to it."

posts.prompt: Write them about a mistake you made that they’ll probably make too.
posts.caption: Most of what your kid inherits from you isn't the good parts. Naming the mistake now, in your own words, is worth more than the warning you'll give later. Write it down while you still remember how it felt.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading LETTER above the prompt: Write them about a mistake you made that they'll probably make too.

posts.prompt: What food are they refusing this week?
posts.caption: The refusals change every few weeks. Pasta was fine in March, now it's an insult. Write down the current one — it's the kind of detail that vanishes the second it ends.
posts.altText: A plain cream card with a small badge reading QUESTION above the prompt text: What food are they refusing this week?

posts.prompt: Photograph the mess they made. Don’t clean it up first.
posts.caption: The clean version isn't the one you'll want in ten years. The blocks where they fell, the crusted bowl, the marker on the wrong surface. That's the shape of who they were that week.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading PHOTO above the prompt text: "Photograph the mess they made. Don't clean it up first."

posts.prompt: Film them explaining how something works.
posts.caption: Ask about the vacuum, or clouds, or why the dog does that. The facts will be mostly wrong. What you're keeping is the hand gestures and the total confidence.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading VIDEO above the prompt text: Film them explaining how something works.

posts.prompt: Record them saying their own full name.
posts.caption: The full name comes out differently at four than it will at nine. Middle name mumbled, last name shouted, or the whole thing said like an announcement. Thirty seconds now, and you'll have the exact shape of it later.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading VOICE above the prompt text: Record them saying their own full name.

posts.prompt: Let them help with something, even though it triples the time.
posts.caption: Three minutes of cracking eggs becomes twelve. You get shell in the bowl and a kid standing on a chair, narrating. Write down what they insisted on doing themselves.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading ACTIVITY above the prompt: "Let them help with something, even though it triples the time."

posts.prompt: Write down the story of the day they were born, in as much detail as you can still remember.
posts.caption: You think you'll never lose this one. Then the hour blurs, and the name of the nurse goes, and the weather that morning. Write it long. The details you think are boring are the ones your kid will ask about.
posts.altText: A plain cream card labeled LETTER, with the prompt: "Write down the story of the day they were born, in as much detail as you can still remember."

posts.prompt: What did they do today that annoyed you and will be funny in ten years?
posts.caption: The stuff that grates now is usually the stuff you retell later. The chair dragged across the kitchen at 6am. The sock worn for the fourth day. Write it down while you still remember which sock.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading QUESTION above the prompt text: What did they do today that annoyed you and will be funny in ten years?

posts.prompt: Take a photo of them sleeping.
posts.caption: You have hundreds of these already. Take one more anyway. The arm flung over the edge, the sock still on, the exact size they were this month.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading PHOTO above the prompt text: Take a photo of them sleeping.

posts.prompt: Record them running toward you.
posts.caption: The run is short and you've seen it a thousand times. But the arms, the sound of the feet, the way they don't slow down at the end — that goes first. Ten seconds is enough.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading VIDEO above the prompt text: Record them running toward you.

posts.prompt: Record them describing you.
posts.caption: You'll hear the details you never noticed you had. The glasses on your head. The way you say their name twice. Fifteen seconds of it, kept.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading VOICE above the prompt text: Record them describing you.

posts.prompt: Don’t rush lights-out tonight. Stay an extra ten minutes.
posts.caption: The talking usually starts after the light goes off. Ten extra minutes in the dark is when you hear about the kid at lunch, or the thing they were scared of last week. Write down whatever comes out.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading ACTIVITY above the prompt text: "Don't rush lights-out tonight. Stay an extra ten minutes."

posts.prompt: Write them something about their mother they’d never think to ask about.
posts.caption: Kids know their mother as their mother. They don't know the person who existed first. Write down one thing from before — a job, a fear, a habit they dropped. It's the kind of detail that never comes up on its own.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading LETTER above the prompt text: Write them something about their mother they'd never think to ask about.

posts.prompt: Who is their best friend right now, and what do they do together?
posts.caption: The name changes. Sometimes by Thursday. Write down what the two of them actually do together — the game with the made-up rules, the corner of the yard — because that's the part nobody remembers later.
posts.altText: Cream-colored card with a small badge reading QUESTION above the prompt: "Who is their best friend right now, and what do they do together?"

posts.prompt: Photograph their drawing or their handwriting, exactly as it is.
posts.caption: The backwards letters go away first. Then the way they hold a marker, the way one leg of the M is longer. Take it before it's neat. Paper fades, and this stuff never makes it to the fridge for long.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading PHOTO above the prompt text: Photograph their drawing or their handwriting, exactly as it is.

posts.prompt: Film the bedtime routine start to finish, one take.
posts.caption: The three-minute stall at the sink. The book they pick every night. The order it all happens in. You'll forget the sequence entirely within a year, and the sequence is the part you'll want back.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading VIDEO above the prompt text: Film the bedtime routine start to finish, one take.

posts.prompt: Record two minutes of dinner. Don’t announce it. Just the room.
posts.caption: The chair scraping, the fork on the plate, the sentence that gets interrupted twice. That's the part you won't remember on your own. Two minutes, unannounced, is enough.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading VOICE above the prompt text: Record two minutes of dinner. Don't announce it. Just the room.

posts.prompt: Say yes to the next thing you’d normally say no to.
posts.caption: Usually it's something small. A second bath, crackers before dinner, the long way home. The yes costs less than you think, and it's the part they'll bring up years later.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading ACTIVITY above the prompt: "Say yes to the next thing you'd normally say no to."

posts.prompt: Write down what you hope they keep from being four years old.
posts.caption: You'll probably start with something big. Then you'll remember the way they narrate their own snacks, and write that down instead. The small one is usually the one that lasts.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading LETTER above the prompt: "Write down what you hope they keep from being four years old."

posts.prompt: What word do they mispronounce that you don’t want to correct?
posts.caption: Every kid has one. Hostibul. Aminal. Bassghetti. It fixes itself in a month or two and you won't be able to remember what the wrong version sounded like. Write it down the way they say it.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading QUESTION above the prompt text: What word do they mispronounce that you don't want to correct?

posts.prompt: Take a picture of them with whoever they’re most attached to right now.
posts.caption: Attachments move. The grandparent, the neighbor's dog, the one kid at school whose name comes up every night. Get them in the frame together while it's true. In a year you'll want proof of who it was.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading PHOTO above the prompt: "Take a picture of them with whoever they're most attached to right now."

posts.prompt: Ask them what they’d say to themself at eighteen. Film it.
posts.caption: Kids answer this like it's a dare, not a legacy. You'll get advice about snacks, or a warning about somebody in their class. Keep the take where they forget the camera is on.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading VIDEO above the prompt text: Ask them what they'd say to themself at eighteen. Film it.

posts.prompt: Record them reading a page out loud.
posts.caption: The stumbles are the part you'll want later. The pause before a hard word, the way they read the punctuation like it's a suggestion. Thirty seconds is enough.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading VOICE above the prompt text: Record them reading a page out loud.

posts.prompt: Let them choose dinner. Entirely.
posts.caption: You'll learn something from what they pick. Usually that the sides matter more than the main, or that two foods must never touch. Write down the menu before you forget it.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading ACTIVITY above the prompt text: "Let them choose dinner. Entirely."

posts.prompt: Write them what you’d want them to know if you weren’t around to say it.
posts.caption: Most parents start with the big thing and end up somewhere smaller. How you take your coffee. The name of the street you grew up on. Which one of their grandparents you got your temper from. Write it down while it's ordinary.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading LETTER above the prompt: "Write them what you'd want them to know if you weren't around to say it."

posts.prompt: What are they afraid of right now?
posts.caption: Fears date a kid faster than photos do. The hallway light. A specific dog two streets over. The sound the dishwasher makes at the end. Write down the one that's current, because in four months it'll be something else entirely.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading QUESTION above the prompt text: "What are they afraid of right now?"

posts.prompt: Photograph their lunch, arranged the way they arranged it.
posts.caption: The crusts pushed to one side. Crackers stacked into a tower. It's a system, and it will be gone by spring. Take the picture before you clear the plate.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading PHOTO above the prompt: "Photograph their lunch, arranged the way they arranged it."

posts.prompt: Film them eating something for the first time.
posts.caption: The face does something you can't write down. Ten seconds is enough. Years later it's the sound you'll want back more than the picture.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading VIDEO above the prompt text: "Film them eating something for the first time."

posts.prompt: Record them telling a joke.
posts.caption: The joke is never the point. It's the wind-up, the part where they lose the thread, the laugh that comes before the punchline. That's the sound you won't be able to reconstruct later.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading VOICE above the prompt text: Record them telling a joke.

posts.prompt: Ask them a question and let the silence sit until they answer it.
posts.caption: Most answers arrive four seconds after we've already filled the gap. Ask, then count to ten in your head. What comes out is usually not the answer you were expecting.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading ACTIVITY above the prompt: "Ask them a question and let the silence sit until they answer it."

posts.prompt: What did they teach themself this month?
posts.caption: Not the milestone kind. The zipping-a-coat, whistling-badly, opening-the-yogurt-alone kind. Nobody taught it, nobody wrote it down, and in six weeks you won't remember it started this month.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading QUESTION above the prompt text: What did they teach themself this month?

posts.prompt: Take a photo of them doing the thing they do every single day.
posts.caption: The daily thing feels too ordinary to photograph. That's why nobody has. In a year the shoes by the door, the same chair, the same grip on the cup will be the part you can't otherwise get back.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading PHOTO above the prompt text: Take a photo of them doing the thing they do every single day.

posts.prompt: Record them dancing to whatever’s playing.
posts.caption: You'll never remember the song. You will remember the way they hold one arm out, or the stomp that isn't on any beat. Ten seconds is plenty.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading VIDEO above the prompt: "Record them dancing to whatever's playing."

posts.prompt: Record them talking about their best friend.
posts.caption: The name comes out about forty times a minute. In two years you won't remember how they said it. Keep the recording short. The talking will not be short.
posts.altText: Cream card with a small badge reading VOICE above the prompt text: "Record them talking about their best friend."
